paragraphs.text: What If the Dinosaur-Killing Asteroid Hit Today?
Start with the assumption. Global heating from falling debris, then years of dimmed sunlight that collapse food chains.
That is the first effect — but not the biggest. Assume a Chicxulub-size asteroid strikes Earth today.

The second-order effect is stranger. One 10-kilometre asteroid ended the age of dinosaurs. Stood on end, it would tower over Everest. It struck slightly over 66 million years ago. The crater it left is up to 300 kilometres wide. Today, the first danger would be heat and debris raining worldwide. Then soot and dust would dim sunlight for years. The real killer wasn't the crater. It was the sky. The Chicxulub crater was formed slightly over 66 million years ago when an asteroid, about ten kilometers (six miles) in diameter, struck Earth. The impactor was around 10 kilometers (6 mi) in diameter, large enough that, if set at sea level, it would have reached taller than Mount Everest. More recent evidence suggests the crater is 300 km (190 mi) wide, and the 180 km (110 mi) ring observed is an inner wall of the larger crater. Field research from the Hell Creek Formation shows the simultaneous mass extinction of myriad species, consistent with the impact event. An impact turns the asteroid's kinetic energy into heat, shock and ejecta; fine debris and soot then block sunlight. A Chicxulub-size asteroid strikes Earth today.
And here is where science stops being certain. The governing physics: an impact turns the asteroid's kinetic energy into heat, shock and ejecta; fine debris and soot then block sunlight.
So what is the answer? The exact timeline depends on how the impossible change happens; the order of effects is what established physics constrains.
